sections.title: What Drives Predictive Analytics Cost
sections.description: Unlike some AI categories where cost is driven primarily by model complexity, predictive analytics cost is driven primarily by data readiness.

items.title: 1. Data Quality and Availability (The Dominant Factor)
items.description: McKinsey's Global AI Survey consistently identifies data quality and availability — not model sophistication — as the primary bottleneck. Outcome labels exist and are clean: fastest to build. Outcome labels require definition and backfill: +$8,000–$20,000. Data is fragmented across systems: +$10,000–$30,000. Limited historical outcome data: most expensive scenario — additional data collection, synthetic augmentation, or modified approaches required.
items.label: Data readiness

items.title: 2. Real-Time vs. Batch Prediction
items.description: Batch prediction (daily scoring runs, weekly updates): Lower infrastructure cost. Suitable for churn prevention, marketing applications. Real-time prediction (scoring at the moment of a transaction/event): Requires low-latency serving infrastructure. Fraud detection, real-time personalization, live loan decisions require real-time scoring. Adds $10,000–$35,000 for serving infrastructure.
items.label: Real-time vs. batch

items.title: 3. Integration Depth
items.description: Predictive analytics that lives in a dashboard nobody checks delivers no ROI. ROI is realized when predictions integrate into workflows where decisions are made. Churn score → Salesforce task: $5,000–$12,000. Fraud score → payment gateway: $8,000–$20,000. Lead score → CRM priority queue: $5,000–$12,000. Equipment failure → maintenance dispatch: $8,000–$18,000.
items.label: Integration

items.title: 4. Explainability Requirements
items.description: Standard ML models produce predictions without built-in explanations. For regulated applications requiring individual-level explanations: SHAP value integration: +$8,000–$15,000. Adverse action reason code generation (FCRA): +$10,000–$20,000. SR 26-2 model validation documentation: +$20,000–$50,000.
items.label: Explainability

items.title: Demand Forecasting
items.description: Retailer, $15M inventory value, 20% overstock + 8% stockout. 30% improvement in forecast accuracy reduces overstock by $900K, stockout-related lost sales by $200K = $1.1M recovered in Year 1. Cost: $50,000–$100,000 | Payback: 1–2 months.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.description: Common questions about predictive analytics development and cost.

items.question: What's the minimum data history needed for a useful predictive model?
items.answer: Depends on the prediction target. Churn models: 12–24 months with several hundred churned examples. Fraud models: enough historical fraud cases to train on rare positive events — typically 1,000+ labeled fraud instances. Demand forecasting: 2–3 years to capture seasonal patterns. ClickMasters assesses your specific situation during Discovery.

items.question: Is $30,000 enough budget for a useful predictive analytics system?
items.answer: For a focused single use case (lead scoring, basic churn) with accessible, relatively clean data: yes. For regulated industry applications (credit, clinical) or complex multi-variable forecasting: budget $50,000–$100,000.

items.question: How accurate can predictive analytics be?
items.answer: AUC-ROC of 0.75–0.90 is typical for well-built churn and lead scoring models with adequate data. ClickMasters validates accuracy on your specific data before deployment.

items.question: What happens when the model's predictions start to degrade?
items.answer: Drift monitoring detects when distribution shift or accuracy degradation exceeds threshold — alerting for retraining. ClickMasters builds this as standard, not as a $15,000 add-on.

items.question: How long does predictive analytics development take?
items.answer: 10–36 weeks depending on scope. Single-use-case with accessible data: 10–18 weeks. Multi-model platform with compliance documentation: 18–36 weeks.

items.question: Is explainability important for our predictive analytics use case?
items.answer: Regulatory contexts (credit, employment, clinical) require individual-level explanations — ClickMasters integrates SHAP as standard for these. For internal operations use cases where regulatory explainability isn't required, SHAP is still useful for model validation and bias detection but not mandatory.
